executive_summary: The defining thread of the day is the contest over institutional legitimacy — who holds power, who abuses it, and what rules actually govern consequential actors. The Musk v. Altman trial, covered in long-form, distills this most sharply: a jury is now being asked to decide which of two men controlling transformative AI technology is lying about the foundational purpose of OpenAI, a fight that is ultimately about whether nonprofit governance constraints mean anything when trillion-dollar stakes are involved. The breaking news reinforces the same thread from a different angle — a federal ICE agent criminally charged for shooting a civilian, and a judge ruling on the admissibility of evidence in the Mangione case, both turning on whether agents of institutional power operated within or outside legal bounds. Google's reported third-place standing in foundation models, flagged in the MIT Technology Review piece, adds a corporate dimension: the company that once defined the AI era is losing legitimacy as a frontier competitor precisely because it cannot demonstrate technical authority where it matters most. Across courtrooms, federal law enforcement, and Silicon Valley, today's news is unified by a single question — when powerful institutions and the individuals who lead them act badly or fall behind, what mechanisms actually hold them accountable?

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?

items.headline: Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?
items.blurb: A year ago I reported on the impact of artificial intelligence on the fight against climate change. On the one hand, data centres used a lot of electricity; on the other, that electricity was mostly renewable, and could be used to develop technologies that helped cut emissions around the world. Overall it felt like cause for cautious optimism, especially if—as we argued in an accompanying leader—AI companies would share more information about the impact of their systems to help consumers make informed decisions. A lot has changed since then. Some shifts were predictable. The amount of electricity the AI industry uses has exploded. The biggest models take more energy to train and run than they did last year, and they are being used by more people to do more things more of the time. Some adjustments were grimly inevitable. Where big tech companies once felt bound by promises they had made in a different political era to cut, or even reverse, their emissions, they now seem happy to switch on new gas turbines to power their growing ambitions, although they still generally insist that the extra energy use is just a temporary measure to compensate for a lack of capacity on the electricity grid. Other changes were more surprising. Last year data-centre impacts felt like a niche topic discussed by people interested in the overlap between AI and climate change. Now they are an increasingly important part of national—and international—politics. In America politicians are proposing regional and national moratoriums on construction, prompting entrepreneurs to wonder whether it might be cheaper to launch computers into space rather than fight through the morass on Earth.

longform.title: Musk v. Altman week 3: now the jury will pick a side
longform.thesis: The third and final week of the Musk v. Altman trial reduced to a credibility contest between two tech titans, with Altman accused of lying and self-dealing and Musk portrayed as a power-hungry actor seeking control over AGI, leaving the jury to adjudicate competing narratives about OpenAI's contested nonprofit status.
longform.context: The article is a newsletter dispatch from MIT Technology Review's May 18, 2026 edition, summarizing courtroom reporter Michelle Kim's coverage of the third week of the Musk v. Altman trial — a case centered on Musk's claims that he was deceived about OpenAI's mission and structure.
arguments: Musk's legal team framed Altman as a liar engaged in self-dealing, attacking his personal credibility rather than focusing solely on contractual or fiduciary claims — a strategy aimed at undermining Altman's characterization of OpenAI's mission as genuinely nonprofit.

Altman's defense countered by portraying Musk as a 'power-seeker trying to control artificial general intelligence,' reframing the lawsuit as a cynical competitive maneuver by the founder of rival AI company xAI rather than a principled grievance.

The trial surfaced new details about OpenAI's contested nonprofit conversion, including an anecdote about a 'golden trophy of a donkey's ass awarded to an employee who challenged Musk' — evidence used to illustrate the internal culture and power dynamics at early OpenAI.
longform.significance: The case is a public referendum on the governance of the most consequential AI organization in the world, with the jury's verdict likely to shape legal and regulatory precedent around nonprofit-to-for-profit conversions in the AI sector. It also exposes the personal and institutional tensions that have driven the fracture between two figures who co-founded OpenAI, lending legal weight to what had previously been a public relations war. The trial lands as broader AI geopolitics intensify, with Chinese labs pulling ahead in video generation and SpaceX preparing a landmark IPO, underscoring how much is at stake in the race Musk and Altman are both racing to win.
questions_raised: Whether the jury will interpret OpenAI's structural transformation as a breach of founding commitments or as legitimate organizational evolution — a question the article does not resolve and one with sweeping implications for AI nonprofit governance.

The article raises but does not address whether Musk's simultaneous operation of xAI, which reportedly 'distills OpenAI's models,' undermines the legal standing or moral authority of his claims against Altman.

longform.title: What to expect from Google this week
longform.thesis: Google enters I/O 2026 as a clear third-place foundation model competitor, with meaningful strength in AI for science but a serious, possibly unrecoverable deficit in the coding capabilities that now define frontier AI status.
longform.context: Written on the eve of Google I/O 2026, the piece responds to months of competitive erosion in which Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex have so thoroughly outpaced Google's coding tools that DeepMind engineers were reportedly forced to use Claude for their own work.
arguments: Google's coding position has deteriorated from near-parity to distant third: a year ago distinctions among top LLMs 'often felt like a subjective splitting of hairs,' but today Google's tools are 'so dramatically superior' — in competitors' favor — that internal engineers fought over Claude access as recently as April 2026, making a two-day conference turnaround implausible.

Science and health remain Google's 'conspicuous strength' — it is the only frontier AI company with a Nobel Prize, and tools like AlphaFold, the AI co-scientist (described as an 'oracle' by a Stanford scientist), and AlphaEvolve represent a sustained lead that LLM commoditization has not erased, even as OpenAI has seized the health AI narrative with ChatGPT Health.

Internal controversy threatens Google's carefully maintained image of neutrality: 600 employees, many from DeepMind, sent Sundar Pichai a letter protesting a DoD deal, which Google signed the following day — a tension that will 'worm its way in' despite on-stage efforts to avoid it, contrasting with CEO Demis Hassabis's deliberate positioning as an apolitical 'Nobel Prize-winning nerd.'
longform.significance: The piece reframes the standard Google I/O narrative — typically framed around consumer product launches — as a competitive triage moment for a company that has lost the metric (coding) that now determines frontier AI credibility. It also surfaces a consequential but underreported divergence: the same company falling behind on coding benchmarks is simultaneously the only one producing Nobel-level scientific AI, raising questions about whether 'frontier' is being defined too narrowly. The internal DoD protest adds a governance dimension that complicates Google's neutrality brand at a moment of heightened scrutiny of AI-military contracts.
questions_raised: Whether Google's Health Coach launch represents 'appropriate caution in a high-stakes domain' or is simply another domain where the company has fallen behind — a distinction with major implications for Google's health AI strategy and its ability to compete with OpenAI's clinical positioning.

Whether the coding deficit is structural (a talent or research culture problem requiring more than a new DeepMind team to fix) or a temporary execution gap that a major I/O release could begin to close — the article implies the former but does not resolve it.
